results.summary: Grain-Flex-FPGA is a small field-programmable gate array with one configurable logic block (CLB) containing four 4-input look-up tables, each with an optional output flip-flop. The CLB has four inputs and four outputs that can be routed to any of eight IO buffers, and each LUT input can be connected to any CLB input or any LUT output. The device is programmed through a scan chain using dedicated clock, reset, enable, and data-in pins, with data-out on a single pin. The SpinalHDL project includes examples for generating bitstreams, but no silicon test results are provided, and the documentation notes that VTR support is still forthcoming.

This project implements a two-player Pong game in Verilog, outputting a 2-bit-per-channel VGA video signal and a sound output. Each player controls a paddle with three buttons (left, right, action), and the game ends when one player runs out of lives. The design uses a VGA timing module and painter modules to generate graphics and detect collisions, with the ball bouncing at different angles depending on where it hits the paddle. It requires a VGA monitor, a VGA DAC built from 2-bit R2R resistor networks, and external buttons; the author reports that the silicon works.

Tiny Breakout is a single-player Breakout game in Verilog that outputs a 2-bit-per-channel VGA video signal and a sound output. The game is controlled by three buttons (left, right, action) and includes an SPI interface for reading the game state and writing commands to modify it. The design uses a VGA timing module, painter modules for graphics, and a shift register to store the 13x16 block grid efficiently. It requires a VGA monitor, a VGA DAC made from 2-bit R2R resistor networks, and external buttons; the author reports that the silicon works.

This design implements a temperature sensor using four ring oscillators whose frequencies vary with temperature. It counts the oscillator cycles over a fixed period of the system clock, accumulates the counts based on a selectable sum factor, and transmits the 3-byte sum over UART when a start code is received. The oscillator counter divided by two is also output on the bidirectional pins and upper output pins. The project is based on a previous Tiny Tapeout design and requires an external clock and UART connection for testing; no silicon test results are provided.

This project is a 12-bit write decodifier for a reservation station, likely part of a CPU design. It takes a 12-bit input on the ui and uio pins and produces a 12-bit output on the uo and uio pins, selecting the appropriate reservation station based on the input. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it works by selecting the corresponding RS needed and that testing involves manipulating input switches to observe outputs. No external hardware or silicon test results are mentioned.

This project implements a 4-bit linear feedback shift register (LFSR) random number generator with configurable feedback polynomials based on a mod input, resetting to an initial state when reset is asserted. The documentation, however, describes a clock divider and binary-to-decimal converter for a 7-segment display, with a 24-bit compare register that defaults to 10,000,000 for a 1-second interval at 10 MHz, and inputs that can override bits 11-18 of the compare value. The bottom 8 bits of the counter are output on the bidirectional pins, and the 7-segment segments are driven on the outputs. The mismatch between the title and the description suggests the documentation may be incorrect or incomplete; no silicon test results are provided.

This project implements a simple Tamagotchi virtual pet game in Verilog that communicates over a serial UART interface. The user connects rx and tx to a serial terminal, and the game starts automatically; the pet has stats for food, sleep, happiness, hygiene, and social, which must be maintained by pressing keys (E, S, P, B, T, W) to feed, sleep, play, clean, talk, or wake up. If the pet dies, the reset button restarts the game. The design requires a 27 MHz clock and a serial terminal; no silicon test results are provided.

This project implements a CDMA transmitter and receiver in Verilog for academic study of spread-spectrum effects and pseudonoise sequences. It uses two 5-bit LFSRs to generate Gold codes, which are used to spread a transmitted signal and to despread a received signal, with a seed input to initialize the LFSRs. The design includes a testbench that simulates transmission and reception, and an LED indicates a valid seed. External hardware includes an operational amplifier for adding noise to simulate a channel, a testboard, and an LED; no silicon test results are provided.

This project is a 7-segment display counter that increments once per second, counting up to 10. It uses a clock divider and combinational logic to convert binary to decimal for the display, with the bottom 8 bits of the counter also output on the bidirectional pins. The counting speed can be adjusted by setting the input pins to override bits 11-18 of a 24-bit compare register; with all inputs zero, the compare is 10,000,000, giving a 1-second interval at 10 MHz. The design requires a 10 MHz clock and a 7-segment display; no silicon test results are provided.

This project is a serializer implemented as a shift register, with a clock, reset, and 6-bit parallel data input, and a single serial output Q plus an end-of-sequence output eos. The documentation is essentially empty, containing only placeholder text for how it works and how to test. No external hardware or silicon test results are mentioned. The functionality is inferred from the pin names and title.
